claim: Glycine and D-serine are endogenous co-agonists that can both play the role of NMDAR co-agonist.
source: It has been established that endogenous glycine and D-serine can both play thid ms role (Oliet and Mothet, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oliet and Mothet, 2009.

claim: D-serine is the endogenous co-agonist at glutamatergic synapses in the adult forebrain.
source: even though D-serine was shown to be the endogenous co-agonist at glutamatergic synapses in the adult forebrain (Papouin et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Papouin et al., 2012.

claim: GluN2B subunits are highly expressed during early development and reach a peak around the second postnatal week.
source: GluN2B subunits are highly expressed during early development and reach a peak around the second postnatal week
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Monyer et al., 1994 and Barth and Malenka, 2001 in the same sentence.

claim: GluN2A subunit levels increase only after birth, exceeding GluN2B subunits by adulthood.
source: whereas GluN2A subunit levels increase only after birth, exceeding GluN2B subunits by adulthood (Monyer et al., 1994; Barth and Malenka, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Monyer et al., 1994 and Barth and Malenka, 2001.

claim: Synaptic NMDAR are mostly gated by D-serine, whereas extrasynaptic receptors are gated by glycine.
source: It recently emerged that synaptic NMDAR are mostly gated by D-serine, whereas extrasynaptic receptors are gated by glycine (Papouin et al., 2012; Sullivan and Miller, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Papouin et al., 2012 and Sullivan and Miller, 2012.

claim: Glycine and D-serine differentially regulate the surface dynamics of NMDAR on hippocampal neurons.
source: it appears that glycine and D-serine differentially regulate the surface dynamics of NMDAR on hippocampal neurons (Burnet et al., 2011; Papouin et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burnet et al., 2011 and Papouin et al., 2012.

claim: Both glycine and D-serine alter NMDAR internalization in a clathrin-dependent mechanism.
source: In addition, both glycine and D-serine alter NMDAR internalization in a clathrin-dependent mechanism (Nong et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nong et al., 2003.

claim: The instantaneous diffusion coefficient of GluN2A-NMDAR was decreased by 14% in presence of glycine.
source: We found that the instantaneous diffusion coefficient of GluN2A-NMDAR was decreased by 14% in presence of glycine, whereas D-serine had no effect (glycine: 86 ± 1% of control, n = 8115 trajectories, p<0.0001; Figure 1b–c; D-serine: 100 ± 2% of control, n = 5555 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule tracking experiments showing quantified diffusion coefficients with statistical analysis.

claim: D-serine had no effect on the instantaneous diffusion coefficient of GluN2A-NMDAR.
source: We found that the instantaneous diffusion coefficient of GluN2A-NMDAR was decreased by 14% in presence of glycine, whereas D-serine had no effect (glycine: 86 ± 1% of control, n = 8115 trajectories, p<0.0001; Figure 1b–c; D-serine: 100 ± 2% of control, n = 5555 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant change in diffusion coefficient with D-serine treatment.

claim: The MSD curves of GluN2A-NMDAR in the presence of glycine or D-serine were undistinguishable.
source: We found that the MSD curves of GluN2A-NMDAR in the presence of glycine or D-serine were undistinguishable (glycine: MSD0.5-0.75s = 0.2135 ± 0.011 µm2; D-serine: MSD0.5-0.75s = 0.246 ± 0.012 µm2; n = 250–252 selected trajectories for each group, p=0.1087; Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing MSD measurements with statistical comparison.

claim: GluN2B-NMDAR surface diffusion was markedly reduced in presence of exogenous D-serine.
source: In contrast, GluN2B-NMDAR surface diffusion was markedly reduced in presence of exogenous D-serine, whereas glycine incubation was without significant effect (D-serine: 57 ± 11% of control, n = 836 trajectories, p<0.001; Figure 1E–G; glycine: 71.5 ± 11% of control, n = 318 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1E–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule tracking showing quantified diffusion coefficients with statistical analysis.

claim: Glycine incubation had no significant effect on GluN2B-NMDAR surface diffusion.
source: In contrast, GluN2B-NMDAR surface diffusion was markedly reduced in presence of exogenous D-serine, whereas glycine incubation was without significant effect (D-serine: 57 ± 11% of control, n = 836 trajectories, p<0.001; Figure 1E–G; glycine: 71.5 ± 11% of control, n = 318 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1E–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant change with glycine treatment.

claim: The diffusion pattern of GluN2B-NMDAR became markedly confined in the presence of D-serine but not glycine.
source: In addition, the diffusion pattern of GluN2B-NMDAR became markedly confined in the presence of D-serine but not glycine (D-serine: MSD0.5-0.75s = 0.042 ± 0.0005 µm2; glycine: MSD0.5-0.75s = 0.107 ± 0.003 µm2; n = 252 selected trajectories for each group; p=0.0022; Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing MSD measurements indicating confined diffusion with D-serine.

claim: Co-agonist treatments did not alter the exchange rate between synaptic and extrasynaptic compartments for GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: These changes were not accompanied by alteration of the exchange rate between synaptic and extrasynaptic compartments (control: 0.056 ± 0.019%, n = 7 neuronal fields, glycine: 0.126 ± 0.044%, n = 4 neuronal fields, D-serine: 0.038 ± 0.015%, n = 7 neuronal fields, p=0.1187; Figure 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing transition ratios with no significant differences.

claim: Neither BsGO nor RgDAAO impacted surface dynamics of GluN2A-NMDAR.
source: We found that neither BsGO nor RgDAAO impacted surface dynamics of GluN2A-NMDAR (BsGO: 124 ± 8.5% of control, n = 308 trajectories; RgDAAO: 96 ± 20% of control, n = 121 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using enzymatic scavengers showing no significant effects on GluN2A-NMDAR diffusion.

claim: Reducing endogenous glycine levels with BsGO decreased GluN2B-NMDAR diffusion coefficient.
source: In contrast, reducing endogenous glycine levels with BsGO decreased GluN2B-NMDAR diffusion coefficient (BsGO: 37.5 ± 12.5% of control, n = 73 trajectories, p<0.05; Figure 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using glycine oxidase showing decreased diffusion coefficient.

claim: The degradation of endogenous D-serine with RgDAAO had no effect on GluN2B-NMDAR diffusion coefficient.
source: The degradation of endogenous D-serine with RgDAAO, on the other hand, had no effect on GluN2B-NMDAR diffusion coefficient, much like glycine application (RgDAAO: 92 ± 5.5% of control, n = 605 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using D-amino acid oxidase showing no significant effect.

claim: The relative content of synaptic GluN2B-QD was strongly reduced by D-serine incubation and degradation of glycine.
source: Consistently, the relative content of synaptic GluN2B-QD, estimated as the synaptic fraction of single GluN2B-QD, was strongly reduced by D-serine incubation and degradation of glycine (D-serine: 62.5 ± 12% of control, n = 14 dendritic fields, p<0.05; BsGO: 36 ± 15% of control, n = 37 dendritic fields, p<0.05; Figure 1J)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantum dot tracking showing reduced synaptic content.

claim: The density of GluN2A-QD remained unaffected by co-agonist manipulations.
source: This effect was specific to GluN2B-QD as the density of GluN2A-QD remained unaffected (n = 12–21 dendritic fields, p>0.05; Figure 1I)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in GluN2A-QD density.

claim: Incubation with glycine or D-serine did not alter the synaptic content of GluN2A-NMDAR.
source: Incubation with glycine or D-serine (45 min, 30 µM) did not alter the synaptic content of GluN2A-NMDAR (113 ± 12% and 100 ± 8% of control for glycine and D-serine, respectively, n = 39–41 cells, p>0.05; Figure 2A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing no significant changes in synaptic GluN2A-NMDAR.

claim: Glycine or D-serine did not alter the total surface amount of GluN2A-NMDAR clusters.
source: and the total (extra- and synaptic) surface amount of clusters (110 ± 9% and 103 ± 7% of control for glycine and D-serine, respectively, p>0.05; Figure 2A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing no significant changes in total surface GluN2A-NMDAR.

claim: Glycine or D-serine did not change the total content of GluN2A-NMDAR under permeabilized conditions.
source: Using the same anti-GluN2A subunit antibody under permeabilized condition, to stain both intracellular and surface GluN2A-NMDAR, revealed no change in the total content (glycine: 97 ± 5%, D-serine 105 ± 5% compared to control, respectively, p>0.05, Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data under permeabilized conditions showing no significant changes.

claim: D-serine reduced the surface synaptic staining of GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: In contrast, D-serine reduced the surface synaptic staining of GluN2B-NMDAR (68 ± 7% of control, n = 39–40 cells, p<0.05; Figure 2D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing reduced synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR with D-serine treatment.

claim: Glycine had no significant effect on surface synaptic staining of GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: whereas glycine was without significant effect (79 ± 7% of control, n = 40 cells, p>0.05; Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing no significant effect of glycine on synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR.

claim: The surface staining of GluN2B-NMDAR was unaffected by glycine or D-serine in all conditions.
source: This was specific to synaptic clusters since the surface staining (extra- and synaptic) of GluN2B-NMDAR was unaffected in all conditions (glycine: 91.5 ± 7%, D-serine: 82 ± 7%, compared to control, Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing no significant changes in total surface GluN2B-NMDAR.

claim: The total content of GluN2B-NMDAR was not altered by glycine or D-serine incubation.
source: The total content of GluN2B-NMDAR, evaluated by the labeling of GluN2B subunits after permeabilization, was not altered by glycine or D-serine incubation (glycine: 103 ± 9%, D-serine: 112 ± 8% compared to control, Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data under permeabilized conditions showing no significant changes.

claim: The total content of GluN1 subunit was unaltered by glycine or D-serine incubation.
source: Furthermore, the total content of GluN1 subunit (staining in permeabilized condition) was unaltered by glycine or D-serine incubation (glycine: total 102 ± 8%, synaptic 101 ± 8%; D-serine: total 94 ± 5%, synaptic 88 ± 5% compared to control, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing no significant changes in GluN1 content.

claim: The GluN2B subunit level in synaptosomes was significantly decreased after D-serine incubation.
source: Consistently, the GluN2B, but not GluN2A, subunit level was significantly decreased after D-serine incubation (glycine/D-serine ratio change relative to control, GluN1 1 ± 10%, GluN2A 10 ± 8%, GluN2B 28 ± 5%, n = 5 independent experiments, Figure 2H–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from synaptosomes showing decreased GluN2B levels with D-serine.

claim: The GluN2A subunit level in synaptosomes was not significantly decreased after D-serine incubation.
source: Consistently, the GluN2B, but not GluN2A, subunit level was significantly decreased after D-serine incubation (glycine/D-serine ratio change relative to control, GluN1 1 ± 10%, GluN2A 10 ± 8%, GluN2B 28 ± 5%, n = 5 independent experiments, Figure 2H–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from synaptosomes showing no significant change in GluN2A levels.

claim: The total amount of GluN2B subunit was not altered by D-serine incubation in synaptosomes.
source: Also, the total amount of GluN2B subunit was not altered by D-serine incubation (control: 1.0 ± 0.11, n = 5 independent experiments; D-Serine: 0.95 ± 0.16, n = 5; glycine: 0.71 ± 0.14, n = 5; p>0.05, ANOVA one followed by Newman-Keuls multiple comparisons test)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing no significant change in total GluN2B content.

claim: The synaptic content of the obligatory GluN1 subunit was unaffected by glycine or D-serine treatment.
source: Finally, the synaptic content of the obligatory GluN1 subunit was unaffected by either treatment, suggesting a stable amount of NMDAR with thus possible redistributions of other NMDAR subunits (e.g. GluN3A/B)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing no change in GluN1 synaptic content, with inference about possible subunit redistributions.

claim: The D-serine-induced decrease in GluN2B-NMDAR diffusion was prevented by TAT-GluN2B15 peptide.
source: Remarkably, both these effects were prevented in the presence of the TAT-GluN2B15 peptide: D-serine no longer altered the diffusion coefficient (101.1 ± 4.03% of control TAT-GluN2B, n = 713 trajectories, p>0.05; Figure 3A–B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using a competing peptide showing prevention of D-serine effects.

claim: TAT-GluN2B15 peptide prevented D-serine from changing the confinement behavior of GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: or changed the confinement behavior of GluN2B-NMDAR (Figure 3C, TAT-GluN2B: MSD0.35-0.55s = 0.1802 ± 0.003 µm2, TAT-GluN2B + D-serine: MSD0.35-0.55s = 0.1740 ± 0.004 µm2, p=0.4206)
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD data showing no significant change with TAT-GluN2B15 peptide.

claim: D-serine decreased the synaptic content of GluN2B-NMDAR in neurons exposed to TAT-NS peptide.
source: As previously observed, D-serine decrease the synaptic content of GluN2B-NMDAR (co-localized with Homer-1c) in neurons exposed 45 min to the TAT-NS peptide (85.3 ± 2.5% of control TAT-NS, n = 38 neuronal fields; Figure 3D–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing decreased synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR with control peptide.

claim: The D-serine effect on synaptic GluN2B-NMDAR content was prevented by TAT-GluN2B15 peptide incubation.
source: however, this effect was prevented by TAT-GluN2B15 peptide incubation (94.7 ± 2.6% of control TAT-GluN2B, n = 70 neuronal fields; Figure 3D–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing prevention of D-serine effects with competing peptide.

claim: TAT-GluN2B15 peptide at 2 µM concentration reduced the binding between GluN2B-NMDAR and PSD-95.
source: Following a 45 min incubation with TAT-NS or TAT-GluN2B15 (2 µM), the number of GluN2B surface clusters that colocalize with PSD-95 clusters was reduced by the TAT-GluN2B15 peptide (TAT-NS incubation, 7.5 ± 0.5 clusters per 10 µm, n = 30 cells, three independent experiments; TAT-GluN2B15: 5.8 ± 0.3 GluN2B clusters per 10 µm of dendrite, n = 30 cells; p=0.0091, t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing reduced colocalization with PSD-95.

claim: D-serine binding, but not glycine, decreased the amount of PSD-95 co-immunoprecipitated with GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: A subsequent Western-blot quantification analysis revealed that the presence of D-serine, but not glycine, decreased the amount of PSD-95 co-immunoprecipitated with GluN2B-NMDAR (glycine: 100 ± 4.9%, n = 10; D-serine: 81.6 ± 2.7% n = 8, p<0.05; Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing reduced PSD-95 binding with D-serine.

claim: D-serine application did not alter the levels of SAP-102 co-immunoprecipitated with GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: The effect of D-serine was specific to PSD-95 since its application did not alter the levels of SAP-102, another MAGUK family protein, co-immunoprecipitated with GluN2B-NMDAR (glycine: 100 ± 9.3%; D-serine: 95.5 ± 6.4% n = 10, p>0.05; Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing no change in SAP-102 binding.

claim: There was no effect of glycine or D-serine on the interaction between PSD-95 and GluN2A-NMDAR.
source: There was no effect of glycine or D-serine on the interaction between PSD-95 and GluN2A-NMDAR (glycine: 100 ± 9.7%; D-serine: 98.1 ± 10.3% n = 8, p>0.05, Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing no change in PSD-95 binding to GluN2A-NMDAR.

claim: Agonist binding to the NMDAR produces conformational changes of the C-terminus.
source: It has recently been shown that the agonist binding to the NMDAR produces conformational changes of the C-terminus (Dore et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dore et al., 2015.

claim: Conformational changes of NMDAR C-terminus modulate the binding to several intracellular partners.
source: and that these changes modulate the binding to several intracellular partners (Doré et al., 2014; Aow et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Doré et al., 2014 and Aow et al., 2015.

claim: NMDA application caused a significant increase in the GluN1-GFP lifetime when co-transfected with GluN1-mCherry.
source: In the presence of NMDA (20 µM, 5 min), and as expected from previous reports (Dore et al., 2015), the lifetime of GluN1-GFP co-transfected with GluN1-mCherry caused a significant increase in the GluN1-GFP lifetime (NMDA: 2.27 ± 0.01 ns, n = 124; Tyrode: 2.23 ± 0.01 ns, n = 291, p<0.05, Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing increased lifetime with NMDA, consistent with previous reports.

claim: D-serine decreased the lifetime of GluN1-GFP co-expressed with GluN1-mCherry.
source: We next assessed the effect of co-agonist applications on the FRET signal and found that D-serine (30 µM, 5 min) decreased the lifetime of GluN1-GFP co-expressed with GluN1-mCherry (baseline: 2,302 ± 19 ps; D-serine: 2,279 ± 20 ps, n = 103, p<0.05; Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing decreased lifetime with D-serine treatment.

claim: Glycine had no effect on FRET efficiency between GluN1-GFP and GluN1-mCherry.
source: while glycine (30 µM, 5 min) had no effect on FRET efficiency (baseline: 2,222 ± 20 ns; glycine: 2,226 ± 19 ps, n = 110, p>0.05; Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing no significant change with glycine treatment.

claim: When cells were pre-incubated with NMDA, subsequent incubation with either co-agonist did not produce any further change of the lifetime of the GluN1-GFP.
source: Interestingly, when the cells were pre-incubated with NMDA (20 µM), the following 5-min incubation with either co-agonist did not produced any further change of the lifetime of the GluN1-GFP (NMDA baseline: 2,309 ± 15 ps; glycine: 2,320 ± 15 ps; NMDA baseline: 2,333 ± 13 ps; D-serine: 2,334 ± 13 ps; p>0.05; Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing no additional changes with co-agonists in the presence of NMDA.

claim: Glycine is the main endogenous co-agonist of NMDAR at CA3-CA1 synapses during the first week of postnatal development.
source: By assessing the extend of inhibitory effect of the scavengers on NMDA-fEPSPs, we confirmed that glycine is the main endogenous co-agonist of NMDAR at CA3-CA1 synapses during the first week of postnatal development and gets gradually replaced by D-serine over the second and third weeks of postnatal development (Figure 5D–F and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data using enzymatic scavengers across developmental stages.

claim: Glycine gets gradually replaced by D-serine over the second and third weeks of postnatal development at CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: By assessing the extend of inhibitory effect of the scavengers on NMDA-fEPSPs, we confirmed that glycine is the main endogenous co-agonist of NMDAR at CA3-CA1 synapses during the first week of postnatal development and gets gradually replaced by D-serine over the second and third weeks of postnatal development (Figure 5D–F and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing developmental changes in co-agonist usage.

claim: In slices from young animals (P10-15), applications of exogenous glycine or D-serine had no effect on the GluN2A-NMDAR content.
source: In slices from young animals (P10-15), when glycine is the major endogenous co-agonist and GluN2B-NMDAR the major NMDAR subtype (Figure 5A–C), we observed that applications of exogenous glycine (100–200 µM, 30 min) or D-serine (50–100 µM, 30 min) had no effect on the GluN2A-NMDAR content (control: 37 ± 3.4% inhibition by zinc; glycine: 36.55 ± 3.43%, p<0.01; D-serine: 36.07 ± 3.64%, n = 7, p>0.05; Figure 5G)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data using zinc inhibition in young slices.

claim: In slices from adults, exogenous glycine application elicited a small decrease in GluN2A-NMDAR content.
source: In slices from adults (>P50), when GluN2A-NMDAR and D-serine predominate, additional D-serine did not modify zinc-induced inhibition but exogenous glycine application elicited a small decrease in GluN2A-NMDAR content (control: 52 ± 2% inhibition by zinc; glycine: 39 ± 2%, p<0.01; D-serine: 51 ± 2% p>0.05, n = 6, Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data using zinc inhibition in adult slices.

claim: In slices from adults, additional D-serine did not modify zinc-induced inhibition of GluN2A-NMDAR.
source: In slices from adults (>P50), when GluN2A-NMDAR and D-serine predominate, additional D-serine did not modify zinc-induced inhibition but exogenous glycine application elicited a small decrease in GluN2A-NMDAR content (control: 52 ± 2% inhibition by zinc; glycine: 39 ± 2%, p<0.01; D-serine: 51 ± 2% p>0.05, n = 6, Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing no change with D-serine in adult slices.

claim: The synaptic content of GluN2B-NMDAR in slices from young animals was strikingly reduced when artificially increasing the availability of D-serine, but not glycine.
source: In contrast, the synaptic content of GluN2B-NMDAR in slices from young animals was strikingly reduced when artificially increasing the availability of D-serine, but not glycine (control: 40 ± 3% inhibition by Ro25-6981; glycine: 36 ± 2.5%, p>0.05; D-serine: 22 ± 2%, p<0.01; n = 6–7; Figure 5I)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data using Ro25-6981 inhibition in young slices.

claim: In adult rats, GluN2B-NMDAR are virtually absent from CA3-CA1 synapses under control conditions or after prolonged incubation with D-serine.
source: Even more strikingly, whereas GluN2B-NMDAR are virtually absent from CA3-CA1 synapses in adult rats under control conditions or after prolonged incubation with D-serine, they contributed to 23 ± 5% of the total synaptic NMDAR population when glycine was exogenously supplied (control: 1.25 ± 2.33% inhibition by Ro25-6981; glycine: 22.65 ± 5.06%, p>0.05; D-serine: 6.36 ± 2.5%, n = 13, p<0.01, Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing minimal Ro25-6981 inhibition in adult slices under control or D-serine conditions.

claim: When glycine was exogenously supplied to adult slices, GluN2B-NMDAR contributed to 23 ± 5% of the total synaptic NMDAR population.
source: Even more strikingly, whereas GluN2B-NMDAR are virtually absent from CA3-CA1 synapses in adult rats under control conditions or after prolonged incubation with D-serine, they contributed to 23 ± 5% of the total synaptic NMDAR population when glycine was exogenously supplied (control: 1.25 ± 2.33% inhibition by Ro25-6981; glycine: 22.65 ± 5.06%, p>0.05; D-serine: 6.36 ± 2.5%, n = 13, p<0.01, Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing increased Ro25-6981 inhibition with glycine in adult slices.

claim: Glycine levels measured in slices were ~40% lower in adults than in pups.
source: This was further fueled by the finding that glycine levels measured in slices using capillary electrophoresis were ~40% lower in adults than in pups, while D-serine content increased by ~50% over the same period of time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by capillary electrophoresis data measuring amino acid levels across development.

claim: D-serine content increased by ~50% from pups to adults.
source: This was further fueled by the finding that glycine levels measured in slices using capillary electrophoresis were ~40% lower in adults than in pups, while D-serine content increased by ~50% over the same period of time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by capillary electrophoresis data measuring amino acid levels across development.

claim: For both GluN2A- and GluN2B-NMDAR, the EC50 values for glycine and D-serine as well as the maximal current amplitudes achieved were indistinguishable.
source: For both receptor subtypes, we found that the EC50 values for glycine and D-serine as well as the maximal current amplitudes achieved were indistinguishable; indicating that neither subtype of receptor is capable of discriminating between the two co-agonists in respect to binding affinity and extent of activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response curve data from recombinant receptors expressed in Xenopus oocytes.

claim: Neither subtype of receptor is capable of discriminating between glycine and D-serine in respect to binding affinity and extent of activation.
source: For both receptor subtypes, we found that the EC50 values for glycine and D-serine as well as the maximal current amplitudes achieved were indistinguishable; indicating that neither subtype of receptor is capable of discriminating between the two co-agonists in respect to binding affinity and extent of activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dose-response data showing no differences in EC50 or maximal currents.

claim: NMDAR surface dynamics modulate NMDAR-dependent synaptic signaling and plasticity.
source: Since NMDAR surface dynamics modulate NMDAR-dependent synaptic signaling and plasticity (Groc et al., 2006; Dupuis et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Groc et al., 2006 and Dupuis et al., 2014.

claim: The NMDAR co-agonists act as major regulators of the NMDAR function through subtype-specific alterations of receptor trafficking.
source: it thus appears that NMDAR co-agonists act as major regulators of the NMDAR function through subtype-specific alterations of receptor trafficking
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing differential effects of co-agonists on NMDAR subtypes.

claim: The developmental up-regulation of D-serine availability at hippocampal synapses reduces the basal surface trafficking of GluN2B-NMDAR.
source: Here, we provide evidence that co-agonist availability plays a direct role in the synaptic composition of NMDAR subtypes through the regulation of GluN2B-NMDAR surface dynamics. These data fuel a model in which the developmental up-regulation of D-serine availability at hippocampal synapses reduces the basal surface trafficking of GluN2B-NMDAR, favoring a higher GluN2A/GluN2B-NMDAR ratio at maturing synapses (Figure 6)
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: The developmental up-regulation of D-serine favors a higher GluN2A/GluN2B-NMDAR ratio at maturing synapses.
source: These data fuel a model in which the developmental up-regulation of D-serine availability at hippocampal synapses reduces the basal surface trafficking of GluN2B-NMDAR, favoring a higher GluN2A/GluN2B-NMDAR ratio at maturing synapses (Figure 6)
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: The NMDAR co-agonists are key regulators of the receptor surface trafficking at hippocampal synapses.
source: Therefore, we postulate that the NMDAR co-agonists are key regulators of the receptor surface trafficking at hippocampal synapses
evidence: The claim is a postulate based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: The synaptic ratio between GluN2A- and GluN2B-NMDAR varies between developmental stages, brain regions, axonal inputs and sensory experience.
source: In the central nervous system, the synaptic ratio between GluN2A- and GluN2B-NMDAR is not uniform but varies between developmental stages, brain regions, axonal inputs and sensory experience (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Yashiro and Philpot, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lau and Zukin, 2007 and Yashiro and Philpot, 2008.

claim: The GluN2A/B ratio influences key processes such as synaptic maturation and adult long-term plasticity.
source: This ratio influences key processes such as synaptic maturation and adult long-term plasticity (Yashiro and Philpot, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yashiro and Philpot, 2008.

claim: PDZ-scaffold proteins (e.g. SAP-102, PSD-95) are differentially involved in the regulation of the GluN2A/B subunit ratio.
